items.title: Brain connectivity in high-traffic regions may shape how multiple sclerosis damages tissue
items.text: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disorder in which the immune system mistakenly turns against the body's own cells. In this case, immune cells attack myelin, a fatty, protein-rich substance that forms a protective coating around nerve fibers. Myelin gives the brain's white matter its characteristic whitish appearance and helps nerve cells communicate with one another. However, the damage does not stop there. MS is also linked to the gradual shrinking or atrophy of gray matter, the brain tissue where most nerve cell bodies are found. As this tissue shrinks, people tend to experience more severe symptoms, including difficulties with movement and thinking.
